verdict.rationale: The catching-up itself is lexically secure. Harpazo (G0726) in 1 Thess 4:17 elsewhere denotes a real spatial seizure to a different location (John 10:28-29, Acts 8:39, 2 Cor 12:2-4, Rev 12:5), so a bodily removal of believers at the Lord's coming is a sound reading of the verb. Tereo ek tes horas (Rev 3:10) is grammatically bivalent between keeping-out-of and keeping-while-in, giving pretrib a real footing. But the two distinctives of the proposition, that this is a SEPARATE event and that a SEVEN-YEAR gap intervenes before a visible return, are not encoded by any lemma. Paul uses one noun, parousia (G3952), for both the gathering in 1 Thess 4:15 and the destruction of the man of lawlessness in 2 Thess 2:8, and orders apostasia (G0646) BEFORE the Day in 2 Thess 2:3 after linking that Day to our episynagoge (G1997) in 2 Thess 2:1. The vocabulary does not lexically encode a two-phase coming with seven intervening years, so the timing claim is supplied by framework rather than by the words. The lexical pattern is genuinely contested, hence disputed.

scripture.force: The Lord himself descends from heaven with a shouted command, an archangel's voice, and the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ rise first. The vocabulary is audible and public, a single complex of arrival, voice, trumpet, and resurrection. The trumpet and command tie this event to the same public-coming language used elsewhere, which the proposition must read as the church-only phase rather than the universal arrival.

Harpagesometha, future passive of harpazo, names a sudden seizure of the living together with the raised dead into the clouds eis apantesin tou kyriou eis aera. The verb's other uses describe real spatial removal to a different location, the wolf snatching the sheep in John 10:12, no one snatching them out of the Father's hand in John 10:28-29, the Spirit catching Philip away in Acts 8:39, Paul caught up to the third heaven in 2 Cor 12:2-4, the male child caught up to God in Rev 12:5. The lemma therefore supports the reality of a bodily removal at the coming. What harpazo does not encode is the TIMING of that removal relative to any tribulation, and apantesis denotes a formal meeting that in ordinary Hellenistic usage describes a delegation going out to escort an arriving dignitary back into the city, which the proposition must override with a different return-pattern.

Paul calls the transformation a mystery, mysterion, signaling a previously hidden revelation that not all will sleep but all will be changed. The mystery vocabulary fits a distinctive event for living believers, which weighs in favor of treating the catching-up as something more than a public destruction of enemies, a real bodily change for the church.

The change happens en atomo, en ripe ophthalmou, en te eschate salpingi, in an instant, in the blink of an eye, at the LAST trumpet. The verb allasso secures bodily transformation. The adjective eschate, last, supplies a temporal marker that sits awkwardly with a catching-up set seven years before the consummation. A reading that calls this trumpet last-of-a-sub-series-for-the-church is not supplied by the adjective itself, it is supplied by framework.

Tereso se ek tes horas tou peirasmou tes mellouses erchesthai epi tes oikoumenes holes is the lexical crux for the pretrib distinctive. Tereo means to guard, keep, watch over. The preposition ek means out of or from. The combination is genuinely bivalent, it can denote either being kept away from the hour entirely before it begins or being preserved through it while it runs. The promise is to keep ek tes HORAS, ek of the hour itself, not merely ek of the peirasmos, which gives the removal reading a stronger footing than a bare 'ek of the trial' would. But tereo is the verb of preservation, not the verb of removal, and the same author elsewhere distinguishes airo ek (take physically out of) from tereo ek (keep from), so the vocabulary cannot by itself adjudicate.

Erchomai palin kai paralempsomai humas pros emauton, I will come again and receive you to myself, fixes the fact of Christ's return and the gathering of his own to be where he is. Paralambano denotes taking-along, often with the connotation of relocation. The verb supports a real reception of disciples to Christ's place. The verse states nothing about the timing of that coming relative to any tribulation, so it grounds the gathering but neither establishes nor excludes a separated pre-tribulation event.

Paul couples the parousia of the Lord and our episynagoge to him, the gathering noun cognate to the gathering verb of Matt 24:31. Hyper tes parousias tou kyriou hemon Iesou Christou kai hemon episynagoges ep auton ties the coming and the gathering into one prepositional phrase. The single noun parousia is used for the same coming whose unveiling destroys the man of lawlessness in 2 Thess 2:8, which the proposition must split into two phases the noun itself does not encode.

Hoti ean me elthe he apostasia proton kai apokalyphthe ho anthropos tes anomias. The conjunction ean me with subjunctive and the adverb proton, first, lexically order the apostasia and the revealing of the man of lawlessness BEFORE the Day of the Lord, a Day Paul has just linked to the parousia and our episynagoge in 2 Thess 2:1. The grammar fixes a sequence in which the church is still on the scene during apostasy and revealing, which complicates a pre-tribulation removal of the church.

Monon ho katechon arti heos ek mesou genetai, only there is one restraining now until he is out of the way. Katecho is polysemous, to hold fast, to possess, to restrain, and the participle ho katechon has no lexically explicit antecedent. The phrase ek mesou genomai is an idiom for being removed from the middle of a situation, but the referent could be the Spirit, civil order, an angel, or another agent, and the lemma does not name the church. The verse is invoked by the proposition but does not lexically supply its content.

Hoti ouk etheto hemas ho theos eis orgen alla eis peripoiesin soterias, God did not appoint us to wrath but to the obtaining of salvation. Orge here names eschatological wrath. The verse secures that believers are not destined for the wrath of God. It does not lexically specify how that exemption is effected, whether by removal before, sealing during, or preservation through, so the verse grounds the exemption but not the mechanism the proposition asserts.

Houtoi eisin hoi erchomenoi ek tes thlipseos tes megales, these are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. The participle erchomenoi with ek presents a great multitude as having passed through, not been removed before, the great thlipsis. The grammar of ek here is clearly through-and-out-of, which weighs against a removal of all believers prior to the tribulation, though pretrib readings classify these as tribulation-period converts distinct from the prior-raptured church.

Eutheos meta ten thlipsin ton hemeron ekeinon, immediately after the tribulation of those days, places the cosmic darkening and the appearing of the Son of Man on an explicit timeline AFTER the thlipsis. Meta with the accusative is a temporal preposition fixing sequence. The next verse gathers the elect with a great trumpet, vocabulary that overlaps directly with the trumpet and gathering of 1 Thess 4:16-17, suggesting one event after the tribulation.

complicating_texts.resolution: The last trumpet, eschate salpigx, lexically marks finality and is hard to reconcile with a catching-up set a defined seven years before the consummation. The adjective eschate by itself reads as the final trumpet, not last-of-a-sub-series-for-the-church. The proposition can be held only by treating last as restricted to a church-specific trumpet series the text does not name, which is precisely why the verdict is disputed rather than affirmed.

The audible command, archangelic voice, and trumpet of God describe an overt arrival event, complicating a hidden removal distinct from the visible return. The same paragraph that supplies the catching-up ties harpazo to this public coming, so the lexis binds the gathering to a public event rather than separating them. The proposition handles this by classifying the church's hearing of this descent as inaccessible to those left behind, a reading the lemmas themselves do not encode.

Ean me elthe he apostasia proton orders apostasy before the Day of the Lord, and that Day is linked in 2 Thess 2:1 to the parousia and our episynagoge. The most natural reading places the church on the scene during the apostasy and revealing. The proposition responds that the apostasia could mean a physical departure rather than doctrinal defection, but the noun's other occurrence in Acts 21:21 and its cognate verb pattern overwhelmingly carry the sense of doctrinal abandonment, not spatial removal, so this rescue is lexically weak.

Meta ten thlipsin places the appearing of the Son of Man and the angelic gathering with a great trumpet after the tribulation. The trumpet and gathering vocabulary overlaps directly with 1 Thess 4. The proposition addresses this by reading Matt 24 as Israel-focused and the Thessalonian gathering as church-focused, a distinction the lemmas do not lexically draw, since both passages use the same parousia and trumpet and gathering vocabulary.

Erchomenoi ek tes thlipseos describes the great multitude as having come out of the great tribulation, that is, through and out of it. The proposition reads these as tribulation-period believers distinct from a previously raptured church, which is not lexically required but is consistent with the absence of ekklesia from Rev 4-19. The reading is defensible but supplied by structural inference, not by the words of Rev 7:14 itself.

variant_units_examined.note: The marked reading at pantes, we shall all sleep versus we shall not all sleep, affects the statement about death but not the timing claim of the proposition, so it carries no impact on the pre-tribulation verdict.
The marked hoti, that or because, in the many dwellings clause is a discourse connector and does not bear on whether the coming is a separated pre-tribulation event.
No major manuscript variant alters the tereso ek tes horas construction. The bivalence is grammatical, not text-critical, so the verdict's disputed status does not turn on any variant reading.

variants.note: The cited anchor verses sit outside the open-cbgm 3 John CBGM sample, so no published ECM apparatus was examined. The variant units present in the bundle do not touch the timing distinctive that the proposition asserts.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads harpazo in 1 Thess 4:17 as a real bodily removal of the church to the Father's house promised in John 14:3, paralambano pros emauton, and treats tereo ek tes horas in Rev 3:10 as preservation OUT OF the hour itself rather than through it, with ek tes horas pointing to absence from the time-period not merely from the trial within it. Adds that 1 Thess 5:9 exempts believers from eschatological orge, that ekklesia is absent from Rev 4-19 across all 19 chapters of the tribulation unfolding while being present in Rev 1-3 and Rev 22:16, and that 2 Thess 2:7 hints at the restrainer being taken ek mesou before the man of lawlessness is revealed. Reads imminence statements as requiring an any-moment expectation that intervening tribulation events would falsify.

Reads the single parousia noun across 1 Thess 4:15, 2 Thess 2:1, and 2 Thess 2:8 as one coming, the trumpet and gathering vocabulary of 1 Thess 4:16-17, 1 Cor 15:52, and Matt 24:31 as one complex of events, and meta ten thlipsin of Matt 24:29 as fixing the appearing AFTER tribulation. Reads 2 Thess 2:3 ean me elthe he apostasia proton as ordering apostasy and the revealing of the man of lawlessness before the Day of the Lord, the same Day Paul has just linked to the gathering. The catching-up of 1 Thess 4 is thus folded into the post-tribulation appearing, with no lexical room for a separated prior event.

Reads the gathering as occurring during the latter part of the tribulation, accepting the shared parousia and trumpet vocabulary while placing the catching-up after the apostasy and revealing of 2 Thess 2:3 but before the climactic outpouring of orge from which 1 Thess 5:9 exempts believers. The lexicon permits a middle-period rapture as well, since harpazo names the event without fixing its placement and tereo ek can be read as preservation from the eschatological wrath specifically rather than from the trial as a whole.

Treats the catching-up as the gathering at the single visible second coming. Tereo ek in Rev 3:10 is read on the John 17:15 pattern of preservation within rather than removal from, even though the verbs differ. The single parousia, the meta ten thlipsin of Matt 24:29, and the unified trumpet-and-gathering vocabulary leave no lexical room for a distinct prior event or a defined seven-year interval, so the proposition is denied as a framework construct rather than a lexically encoded teaching.

hermeneutics.notes: The competing readings turn on whether harpazo and tereo ek encode a TWO-PHASE coming separated by a defined interval, or whether they describe the church-pertinent dimension of a single parousia. The vocabulary itself does not rank the two patterns. Pretrib has a genuine lexical footing in harpazo as real spatial removal and ek tes horas as the strongest single phrase for keeping out of a time-period, but the canon's single return-vocabulary and 2 Thess 2:3's apostasy-first ordering work against a clean prior removal of the church.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Scripture teaches that living and dead believers are gathered to Christ at his coming. The question under test is whether this gathering is a distinct event occurring before a defined tribulation period and prior to a separate visible second coming, or whether the gathering coincides with a single visible coming at or after the tribulation.
stem_audit.notes: The stem encodes specific framework claims, a seven-year tribulation period and a removal that is distinct from and prior to the visible coming. Both the seven-year duration and the two-phase structure are framework constructs not lexically supplied by any anchor lemma. The verdict is derived on the original stem, with the neutralized form separating the lexically secure gathering from the framework-supplied timing so the dispute is located precisely at the sequencing question.

lay_summary: When the Lord comes, the verses behind this question clearly teach that believers who have died are raised and believers who are alive are suddenly caught up to meet him, and that living bodies are changed in an instant. The Greek verb harpazo in First Thessalonians four seventeen means to seize or snatch away. Its other uses describe real spatial removal to a different place, a wolf seizing sheep, the Spirit catching Philip to another town, Paul caught up to the third heaven, the male child caught up to God in Revelation twelve, so it lexically supports the reality of a bodily removal of believers when Christ comes. The strongest single support for a removal BEFORE a defined tribulation is Revelation three ten, kept FROM the hour of the trial that is about to come on the whole inhabited world. The small Greek word ek means out of or from. Paired with the noun hour, it is the strongest phrase in the New Testament for keeping someone out of an entire time-period, not just out of a danger within that period. That gives a pre-tribulation reading a real footing the words themselves supply. But two things keep the proposition contested. First, the apostle Paul uses one and the same noun, parousia, for the coming that gathers believers and for the coming that destroys the man of lawlessness, and he says in Second Thessalonians two that the Day of the Lord, which he has just linked to that gathering, does not come unless apostasy comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed. The grammar puts the church on the scene during those events. Second, the trumpet and gathering vocabulary of First Thessalonians four matches the trumpet and gathering vocabulary of Matthew twenty-four, which Matthew explicitly places AFTER the tribulation. The words secure a real catching-up and a real keeping-from-the-hour, but they do not lexically encode a two-phase coming with a seven-year gap. Because the timing claim is supplied by larger interpretive frameworks rather than by any single lemma, the lexical evidence is recorded as disputed.
